content: The document outlines the World Health Organization's (WHO) guidelines for stopping mass drug administration (MDA) and verifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis (river blindness), a parasitic disease caused by Onchocerca volvulus. This disease, transmitted by black flies (Simulium species) that breed in fast-flowing rivers and streams, affects the skin and eyes. It is endemic in 31 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, three countries in Latin America, and Yemen. Since 2013, WHO has verified the elimination of onchocerciasis in three Latin American countries. The primary intervention strategy for controlling onchocerciasis is mass drug administration (MDA) with ivermectin. In Africa, annual community-directed treatment with ivermectin is the main approach, with some areas implementing semi-annual treatment. In the Americas, semi-annual ivermectin treatment with at least 85% coverage is standard, with quarterly treatment introduced in some areas. Onchocerciasis control programs using MDA typically progress through three phases: 1. Phase 1 (Treatment Phase): This phase involves regular ivermectin treatment with at least 80% therapeutic coverage. Some countries, such as Equatorial Guinea, Uganda, and Tanzania, supplement MDA with vector control. 2. Phase 2 (Post-Treatment Surveillance): This phase begins immediately after the treatment phase and typically lasts 3–5 years. It involves monitoring to confirm the interruption of transmission. 3. Phase 3 (Post-Elimination Surveillance): This phase starts after the 3–5 years of post-treatment surveillance and confirms that transmission has been permanently interrupted (eliminated) in a country. The guidelines emphasize the use of diagnostic tests to monitor progress and verify elimination. These include: Entomological evaluation using O-150 PCR testing: This test detects the presence of infective-stage larvae (L3) of O. volvulus in black flies. A minimum of 6,000 black flies must be tested from a transmission zone, and all must be free of infective larvae to meet the 95% confidence interval threshold. Serological evaluation using Ov-16 testing: This test detects IgG4 antibodies to the O. The threshold for elimination is less than 1% seropositivity. Parasitological evaluation using skin snip microscopy and DEC patch tests: These methods can monitor progress during the treatment phase but are not recommended for verifying elimination. The guidelines also provide recommendations for stopping MDA and verifying elimination: 1. To demonstrate interruption of transmission for stopping MDA: Use O-150 PCR testing in black flies (strong recommendation, high certainty of evidence). Use Ov-16 serology testing in children under 10 years (strong recommendation, low certainty of evidence). Avoid using skin snip microscopy, except during a transition to Ov-16 serology, where both methods may be used in parallel (conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). Do not use ocular infection assessment to demonstrate transmission interruption (strong recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 2. To confirm interruption of transmission at the end of post-treatment surveillance: Use O-150 PCR testing in black flies (strong recommendation, high certainty of evidence). Use Ov-16 serology testing in children when O-150 PCR results are near the threshold (conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). Avoid using ocular infection assessment (strong recommendation, low certainty of evidence). The guidelines outline standard operating procedures for stopping MDA, including selecting sentinel villages near vector breeding sites and ensuring continuous MDA implementation with at least 80% therapeutic coverage during the treatment phase. An independent oversight committee should be established to advise on stopping MDA and transitioning to post-treatment surveillance. The committee should consider cross-border risks and the status of treatment for other diseases, such as lymphatic filariasis, when determining the length of post-treatment surveillance. The document also highlights the importance of evidence-based recommendations and adherence to international standards for guideline development. The recommendations were formulated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, which assesses the certainty of evidence and balances the benefits and harms of interventions. External peer review was conducted before finalizing the guidelines. In summary, these guidelines provide a comprehensive framework for achieving and verifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis through MDA and post-treatment surveillance. They aim to assist policymakers, national programs, and stakeholders in endemic countries in transitioning from treatment to elimination and ensuring sustained success.
